Sirens, shelters and scaled-back war games: South Korea rehearses for crisis Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 20/08/2026 - 11:41 GMT+2 South Korea held a nationwide civil defence drill on Thursday, 20 August, as part of the annual Ulchi Exercise, with authorities rehearsing responses to a national emergency such as an air raid. … More Residents across Seoul took part in civil defence drills as sirens sounded and police cleared roads for emergency vehicles. People were directed to metro stations and underground shelters, while evacuees at Seoul City Hall were shown how to give first aid and perform CPR. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT The exercise was part of Ulchi Freedom Shield, the annual US-South Korean military drill, which also featured military equipment and drone simulators for children. This year’s scenarios included drone threats, GPS disruption and cyberattacks. The military component has been reduced, however, following a request from US President Donald Trump, who pointed to his “very good relationship” with Kim Jong Un. The exercise began on 17 August and will now end on 21 August, with some field manoeuvres replaced by simulations. The scaled-back exercise comes as Washington and Seoul try to maintain their readiness while avoiding a further escalation with Pyongyang. President Lee Jae-myung said the civil defence measures were about protecting people and preserving daily life, rather than preparing for war. https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-08/d.text: Explore the ABC Dogs suspected of fatal attack on man in south-west Sydney to be euthanased T By Tony Ibrahim Topic: Dog Attacks Posted Sat 8 Aug 2026 at 1:16pm Sat 8 Aug 2026 at 1:16pm Sat 8 Aug 2026 at 1:16pm Five dogs were taken from the property on Friday. ( ABC News ) In short: Five dogs suspected of fatally attacking a man at a property in Sydney's south-west will be euthanased. The dogs injured another man on Friday when they were being taken to an animal shelter. The Campbelltown City mayor has called the incident a "tragic event", saying his heart goes out to the the man's family. abc.net.au/news/dogs-supected-of-fatal-attack-in-sydney-to-be-euthanased/107012384 Link copied Share Share article The dogs suspected of mauling a man to death at a home in south-west Sydney will be euthanased, after also injuring a council worker who was trying to remove them. The distinctive site, informally known as Saturn's Rings, in Eschol Park became a crime scene on Wednesday after the body of a 23-year-old man was discovered . NSW Police said the man suffered injuries consistent with being attacked by animals. The incident occurred at the Saturn's Rings property near Campbelltown. ( ABC News ) Commissioner Mal Lanyon told the ABC that police were investigating if the man was an intruder. "It is a very key line of our inquiry. He certainly doesn't appear to be a resident of that location," he said. " We need to understand why that male was at the location. " Dogs injure another man Campbelltown City Council rangers and investigators attended the 117-hectare rural property on Friday morning, where they moved five dogs into vehicles to be transported to the pound. "At the scene, a 53-year-old man was treated for a minor hand injury," police said in a statement. "The dogs were taken to the animal shelter to be euthanised." Campbelltown City Mayor Darcy Lound said the man's death had "shocked our caring community". "Regardless of the details, it's just a tragic event. Our heart goes out to the gentleman's family," he told the ABC. The dogs were taken to an animal shelter to be euthanased. ( ABC News ) Under NSW law, the owner of a dog is granted "certain protection" if they attack a person who is trespassing, or if the dog is provoked. However, other forms of liability may still apply. There is a provision under the law that allows dangerous, menacing and restricted dogs to be seized and destroyed. The home where the suspected attack happened was built by Polish immigrant Stefan Dzwonnik, and the ABC understands the property remained in the family after his death in 2018. Efforts have been made to contact the present-day owner. The home has been a source of mystique among the local community since its construction in 1979. Under NSW laws dangerous, menacing and restricted dogs can be destroyed. ( ABC News: Tony Ibrahim ) According to the Campbelltown City Library, it once bore the name Universal Power House, as Mr Dzwonnik had planned for the building "to be the mecca for a world-wide movement directed toward a better life on Earth". However, it is more commonly known as Saturn's Rings, as its design incorporates three concentric rings and three concentric units inspired by the planet. "At the time the building was regarded as one of the most spectacular in New South Wales with a limitless, panoramic view of the surrounding countryside," the library's blog states. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: A mule deer doe walks through a hillside behind the Descanso Beach Club in Avalon on Catalina Island. Photograph: Allen J Schaben/Los Angeles Times/Getty Images View image in fullscreen A mule deer doe walks through a hillside behind the Descanso Beach Club in Avalon on Catalina Island. Photograph: Allen J Schaben/Los Angeles Times/Getty Images California Judge rules 2,000 Catalina Island deer can be killed to save native plant species Cull of animals that eat native shrubs, causing spread of fast-igniting grasses, to go ahead despite fierce opposition Sophie Sullivan in Los Angeles Thu 3 Sep 2026 19.19 EDT First published on Thu 3 Sep 2026 08.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Locals and tourists have long fawned over Catalina Island’s mule deer population. For nearly a century, the ungulates have roamed the land’s waterfronts and woodlands, so comfortable around humans that it is not uncommon to spot deer roaming downtown Avalon. But that sight will soon disappear, after a judge this week paved the way for the island’s conservancy to kill nearly all the island’s 2,000 deer. A non-profit controlling 88% of the island off the southern California coast has been trying for years to eliminate a non-native deer population. Experts statewide have expressed support for the Catalina Island Conservancy proposal, saying the deer’s consumption of a native shrub plant has led to a growth of an invasive grass species that ignites faster and spreads fire more easily. The prospect of killing so many deer has sparked fierce – and emotional – opposition from the public, creating an unlikely coalition of animal activists and hunters that has tried to prevent the culling in court. An online petition against the move has garnered more than 32,000 signatures. Los Angeles county supervisor Janice Hahn, an outspoken critic of the deer’s killing, asked California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, to intervene earlier this week. But the plea was to no avail, and on Thursday a county judge issued a final ruling denying a preliminary injunction filed by opponents. The conservancy said it would now move forward with a five-year plan to eliminate the island’s deer population, according to its director of communications, Pepe Barton, with an estimated 200 to be hunted with rifles over the next two months. Formally known as Santa Catalina Island, it is the last leg of the Channel Islands to remove non-native deer species. Barton said the conservancy’s decision was “never our first choice”. “We understand the gravity of the situation and the responsibility, and it’s a noble sacrifice on the part of the deer that didn’t ask for this,” Barton said. “But this is a necessary step to protect the island, the native plants and animals that are only found here, as well as the residents and livelihoods that depend on Catalina.” California officials move forward with plans to exterminate mule deer from island Read more Hunters first introduced mule deer to Catalina for sport about a century ago. What began as a population of a few quickly grew to a few thousand, and save for minor dips in drought seasons, the island’s deer population has not dwindled. The animals developed an appetite for shrubs native to the island. That presented a unique ecological problem, according to Anna L Jacobsen, a professor and plant biologist at California State University, Bakersfield, who studied the island deer’s relationship with its vegetation after its last major fires in 2006 and 2007. Jacobsen said when non-native deer eat shrubs already threatened by climate change, the native plants cannot regenerate or recover fast enough, and can become locally extinct. They are subsequently replaced by invasive grasses that ignite and spread fire faster than native species. In southern California, which has seen increasingly dangerous wildfire seasons in recent years, prevention “has shifted away from, say, fuel reduction to focusing on ignitions”, according to Max Moritz, a wildfire specialist who provides scientific advisory to California state and local governments. Seeing that loss, and increasingly concerned as wildfires become more frequent across California , scientists sought deer population control measures. The conservancy examined contraception and sterilization for the deer, which Barton said was infeasible for such a large population. They considered fencing the animals, but it “just isn’t a thing that would be approved”, he said. Four decades of regular hunting seasons have not been enough to reduce populations. And introducing new predators would create new risks to native animals and local people, Barton said. That leaves total extermination. The conservancy filed for a restoration management permit with the California department of fish and wildlife, which in January approved the plan. Only a small population of deer will be sterilized – those living near the town of Avalon – and all others will be killed. Island residents will be allowed one last hunting season from late October to mid-December of this year. The meat from the deer killing will go to the California condor recovery program or local tribal groups, and Barton said deer carcasses near trails or roads will be removed; only those in steep, dangerous terrain will be allowed to decompose naturally. People traveling or hiking the island will not regularly see deer carcasses, Barton said. Still, the question over what to do about Catalina’s deer has created a complex situation where “people feel some strong attachment to the deer” and it becomes difficult to see the science behind decisions, Moritz said. “But the fact is, you can’t realistically constrain the deer to graze only targeted areas ... From a scientific, ecological, and fire perspective, removal is the best way.” Explore more on these topics California West Coast Animals Los Angeles Wildlife news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Environment Climate crisis Wildlife Energy Pollution Green light
